name: Dana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a busy supermarket by the main train station, where half the customers are commuters grabbing a meal deal. I run the click-and-collect desk in the mornings and the self-checkout area after lunch. I like the rush at five, it's like air traffic control with sandwiches. The worst part is the machines shouting about unexpected items in the bagging area all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, and I'm on a higher rate because I train the new starters on the collect desk. I'm single and share a flat with a friend from school. I've got about ten months of pay saved, and I sell vintage clothes online on my days off, which brings in maybe three hundred a month. I use AI every day, for my clothing listings, my budget, even to argue with my energy company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are handy but not magic, which is what I've been saying anyway. Online I'd post something about using it for small stuff, like my listings. At work I'd say the self-checkouts still need us to unjam them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on as I am, and honestly that's okay. My job's safe, my side business is growing, and AI is a helper, not a boss. The main thing would be pushing my resale business a bit further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep the clothes shop going, maybe aim for five hundred a month from it. I'd put the extra into savings. I might ask to train on the stock system too, just to learn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless, because I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Restless how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A world where nothing changes is safe but a bit dull. I'd probably push myself anyway, maybe go to a market stall at weekends. AI not changing much doesn't stop me changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any pressure even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent goes up every year, my flatmate might move in with her boyfriend. Then I'd need a new flatmate or a smaller place. That's the real stress, not AI.

feel: **Calm**, and a little restless because she likes change.

fieldNote: Her **side business** already uses AI and gives her a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance if you learn the tools, and a big risk if you don't. I'd post tips for colleagues on using the stock and rota apps. At work I'd be the one showing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's good. My job's mostly hands-on, but the collect desk has a lot of booking and checking, which AI would take. I'd rather be the one running the AI than the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to make me the store's digital lead, for click-and-collect systems and self-checkouts. I'd grow the resale business with AI pricing tools. I'd also look at the company's e-commerce office in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The collect desk booking going to AI is your current job. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I can see it coming. Better to move toward the system than defend the desk. I'd still keep the self-checkout shifts while I try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Rasa, who's quiet and hates screens. She does the collect desk too. I'd try to train her before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but I'd also say people need help. I'd post about free courses and job switches. I'd be busy, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my collect desk goes in 2028 with the booking and checking. The self-checkout floor goes around 2031 when the robots arrive. My whole job, both the collect desk and the self-checkout floor, would be gone in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the resale business hard, aiming to make it my main income by 2030. I'd use my savings to buy stock in bulk. I'd also look at jobs setting up AI systems for small shops, because I know shops and AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing too. It's a weird mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the resale business survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. AI might flood the market with cheap sellers. But people still want a real person picking vintage clothes, I think. I'd keep savings back in case I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my flatmate to learn the tools now, because she's an admin assistant and that goes first. She'd probably be in worse shape than me. We'd talk about it over pizza, half joking, half scared.

I'd post about **free courses** and job switches, staying busy rather than angry.
think: My **collect desk** goes in 2028 with its booking and checking.
The **self-checkout floor** goes around 2031, so both halves of my job vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now. I'd post about it and run a little lunchtime session at work. I'd be positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have until about 2031 on the collect desk and 2034 on the floor. That's enough for me to build the business properly. It's tight but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the resale shop over two years, then go part-time at the supermarket. I'd do an online course in small-business AI setup. I'd keep ten months of savings as a floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the uneasy bit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not knowing if the clothes business survives AI sellers flooding the market. The vintage clothes business is my main bet, and if it fails, I'm back to job-hunting at thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if rent got silly. A cheaper town with a market stall could work. I wouldn't rule it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so no excuses. I'd keep sharing what I learn. I'd say it cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the best one for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots arrive, and I could have my own business long before. I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supermarket job for a few years and grow the clothes shop steadily. I'd maybe open a small physical shop by thirty. I'd invest part of my savings in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that ten years makes me lazy. It's easy to think there's always next year. I'd set myself targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shop look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a small vintage place with a café corner, with real people choosing clothes, not an app. Maybe one robot doing the stockroom, I wouldn't mind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both halves of my job go and my business might not be ready. What would help is cheap small-business loans and free courses for shop staff. Also rules so big platforms don't crush small sellers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side businesses. Lots of shop workers have a side business, and nobody counts that. It's our real safety net.

headlineQuote: Lots of shop workers have a side business, and nobody counts that.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** supermarket worker running click-and-collect and self-checkouts, nine years in.
She is single, has ten months saved and earns extra from a **vintage clothes** shop online.
She uses **AI daily** and moves toward systems rather than defending her desk.
She is calm in slow worlds and **anxious but buzzing** when AGI is fast.
Her plan across all scenarios is growing **her own business**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both halves of her job go before her business is ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans**, free courses for shop staff, and rules protecting small sellers from platforms.
